h: Five months under siege and a twin across the water
p: Pendennis wasn't built alone. Across the mouth of the Carrick Roads, St Mawes Castle was put up at the same time, and the two were designed to work as a pair, catching any enemy ships in a crossfire. On a clear day you can see St Mawes from the ramparts, and it's well worth hopping on the ferry from Falmouth to visit it too.

The Civil War siege of 1646 is the big story. The Royalist garrison, led by the elderly Colonel John Arundell, held out for around five months against Parliamentarian forces by land and sea. By the end they were starving, and they finally surrendered in August, one of the last Royalist strongholds in England to fall. They were allowed to march out with full honours, which says a lot about how stubborn the defence had been.

Jump forward to the twentieth century and you'll find a different kind of history. The Half Moon Battery and its gun positions guarded Falmouth during the Second World War, and exploring these more recent defences gives you a real sense of how the castle stayed on duty for centuries.
Allow two to three hours to explore properly.

Back in Falmouth, the National Maritime Museum Cornwall on Discovery Quay is a great follow-up, especially on a wet day. Gyllyngvase Beach is a short walk from the castle if you fancy a paddle, and ferries from the town head over to St Mawes and Flushing. The town's seafaring past runs deep: for over 150 years, Falmouth was home to the Packet Service, fast ships carrying mail across the world. Further up the River Fal, the National Trust's Trelissick has gardens and woodland with lovely river views.
